utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Sayers: [Contd.]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Grubesic.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We had reached paragraph 15 of your outline, and you just described for us, before we broke yesterday, the results of the first free elections in Busovaca municipality and the appointments that were made of Croats and Muslims to various posts in the municipal government. Could you just give the Trial Chamber a feel, at least in your view, Mr. Grubesic, of how well the municipal government functioned in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should like to say that the municipal government, in addition to Croats and Muslims, included also Serb representatives, and that government, made of Croats and Muslims and Serbs from three coalition parties, in my view, in 1991, functioned very well indeed, and it had begun resolving some acute municipal problems which had not been solved for many years before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Proceeding on to the next paragraph, sir. You, as we've heard, were a member of the national parliament in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the beginning of 1991, and it's true, I believe, that you spent several days per month in Sarajevo when parliament was in session.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spent several days at the session of the parliament of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your outline, you say you witnessed the growing Bosnian crisis during the time that you were a Member of Parliament. In your own words, could you just elaborate upon that for Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in point of fact, that is where the Bosnian crisis began or, rather, that is where we witnessed a crisis of the dissolution of Yugoslavia. It all found its reflection in the political life and, therefore, in the parliament. That is, one could see there too that there were different political options upheld by different political parties regarding the future status of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, whether it will become an independent state or a state which would remain in Yugoslavia. There were also different options regarding the internal organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina in case it won its independence. All in all, I can say that the deputies in the parliament of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the SDS ranks, throughout their work in the parliament, were seeking for a way not to answer any of these questions, that is, either of the future status of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the future internal organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you elaborate upon this subject for us, please, the actions, parliamentary actions of the SDS or Serbian Democratic Party representatives in the parliament. Did they contribute to the effective operation of parliament or did they obstruct it? Could you give us your view on that, sir.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my impression was that representatives of the Serb Democratic Party would come to the parliament ready, prepared in advance to talk about anything, simply to dodge devising any solution. They would come with strings of long speeches and thus obstructed the work of the parliament of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We'll skip very briefly over paragraph 18, Your Honours. There's already been a lot of evidence about the JNA offensives in Slovenia and Croatia and the attack upon Ravno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of these events certainly riveted your attention, Mr. Grubesic, would that be fair to say? There's no need to elaborate upon that, but you were aware, and very much aware, of the outbreak of war in Slovenia and Croatia shortly after those republics had declared independence and how the effects of that war trickled over into your country with the attack on Ravno.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You have described it just right. I must say that the news about the attack of Yugoslav People's Army on Slovenia I heard in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because a colleague --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Grubesic, there's no need to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. I'll move on, Your Honour. I know the Court has heard a lot about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it also be fair to say, just summarising paragraph 19, about which there's already been a lot of evidence, that the perception among the Bosnian Croats was that notwithstanding these threats, the preparedness of the Muslim community to consider measures to organise their own defence or the defence of their communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina was limited or non-existent in the Bosnian Croat view?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could say that the Muslim leadership seemed to vacillate or, rather, they were not quite sure whether Bosnia-Herzegovina should stay in the then already rump Yugoslavia or whether to proclaim the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. For those reasons, the Muslim leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina even said that the Yugoslav People's Army was the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that it would protect the sovereignty, integrity, and so on of Bosnia-Herzegovina. For those reasons, I suppose adequate preparations for the defence against the aggression were not carried out. The Croats realised this danger. They were the first ones to have it brought home to them, and realised that there should be a referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina so that Bosnia-Herzegovina could become independent. There were, therefore, several initiatives in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina proposed by the representatives so as to put on the agenda the decision on the referendum on independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'm referring to the latter half of 1991. At that time, the war in Croatia was escalating. There were an increasing number of casualties and destruction in Croatia, and it was only a matter of days when Bosnia-Herzegovina would be attacked by the JNA, hence these initiatives the Croat Democratic Union in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is, those were the ideas of --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could just interrupt you for a minute. It would help if you could give shorter answers to these questions. We'll get through the outline a lot more quickly, and you'll be through with your testimony. Let me just focus your attention on one thing, though. You mentioned the independent referendum but I'd like to ask you some questions about before the referendum. Was there any consideration before the referendum and while the future of your country was still up in the air, was there any consideration given to the Croats considering a secession option, if you like, from Bosnia-Herzegovina, which would be part of, as you described it, a rump Yugoslavia? Was that concept at all considered or discussed amongst you and your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in fact, I told you there were discussions about a referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is what I could hear among -- in the official circles among the deputies and politicians that I had the opportunity to meet. It seems to me that there were some ideas that Croats toyed with the idea that in case Bosnia-Herzegovina remained a rump Yugoslavia, then some thought that the Croats would be entitled, if Bosnia-Herzegovina remained in rump Yugoslavia, that then parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina should secede and join the Republic of Croatia. So that was an idea voiced by some people before the decision on the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was adopted. After that, following that, I did not hear such ideas again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Moving on to the next subject in paragraph 20, could you tell us, sir, the circumstances under which the Travnik Regional Community was formed and what exactly that organisation was organised to fulfil. What function that organisation was organised to fulfil.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could briefly say that the idea about the coordination of work on municipal points of the Croat Democratic Union in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in that area, in the area of Central Bosnia came sometime in the latter half of 1991 because we wanted to coordinate the municipal branches of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina so as to facilitate the preparation for the following period, and the assessments were all quite clear and nonambiguous. All the facts are pointing one direction that war would happen in Bosnia-Herzegovina so one had to prepare oneself in order to prevent the destruction of property and death of a large number of people, and I believe that was the principal reason why this regional community of the HDZ was done or why this coordination was undertaken. It wasn't an official formed Croatia of the Croat Democratic Union, it was simply an initiative of municipal boards for the coordinated activities in that area of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We've also heard a lot in this trial about the formation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the HZ HB. Could you tell the Trial Chamber about what you know about the circumstances under which this organisation was formed and what it stood for, sir.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was like this, I wished to point out that formerly the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna on the 18th of November, 1991, that was when we saw on television horrific scenes, horrible scenes of devastation and the killing of people in Vukovar. That they said at the time when the aggression in the Republic of Croatia culminated at that time, in major casualties. The Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina were realising the danger of war, wanted to organise itself in a community which they called the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and its task was to protect the national rights of Croats and prepare the people for the defence against the Serb aggression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, this organisation was formed, as you said, on the 18th of November, 1991. Could you tell us what the organisation actually did if you know, if anything, between the date of its formation and the spring of 1992 when the Croat Defence Council or HVO was formed?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am not conversant with any note-worthy activities of the Croat community until that time, until spring of 1992, and I do not think it was very active in some specific terms until that time. I think that if it was organised, what it was trying to do was coordinate the activities of the municipalities in the preparation of the defence. And here I should like to point out one more fact, and that is that the constitutionality and justification for the establishment of that community was discussed in the parliament. Rather, I do not know if there was time to discuss it in the parliament, but I do know that as a member of the legislative commission of the parliament, there was a paper at a session of the commission and this paper said that the Croat community had been founded in conformity with the constitution with the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me just skip over the balance of paragraph 21 of the outline because it's covered on paragraph 25 and more appropriately dealt with chronologically when we get there. Let me just turn you to the independence referendum, sir. You've referred to your outline to the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina parliament on January 25th, 1992 where the independence issue was discussed. Could you just tell the Court a little bit about that session, sir, and what went on at it.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was a historic session of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In my assessment, I think it was one of the most important sessions in the history of the parliament in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was a very long session because it was being obstructed by the SDS to prevent the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And in the end, after the speech by the president of the SDS, Karadzic, and he delivered a very heavy speech in the parliament, representatives of the Serb Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina left the parliament, and the representatives of other political parties remained in the parliament and until late in the night, that is, in the morning discussed the decision on the referendum and at long last adopted such a decision; that is, they took the decision to hold a referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We've also heard quite a bit, Mr. Grubesic, about the concepts of constituent peoples and constitutive parts of nations and the role which those two concepts played in the Ravno question being debated amongst the Croat political community at the time of this legislative session. Could you give the Court a feel for the kinds of discussions that were going on in the national parliament about these particular concepts and whether there was agreements upon those concepts between the Croat politicians and the Muslim politicians in the parliament, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the Muslim politicians in Bosnia-Herzegovina, following the recognition of the independence of Slovenia and Croatia, received a clear signal from the International Community that they could hold a referendum on the independence in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The decision to hold the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina also had the agreement of the Croat Democratic Union and the Party for Democratic Action. There was no question of that. However, the dispute arose regarding the definition of the referendum question, which would include not only the future independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina but also the question or, rather, the decision as to the internal organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the years to come. Representatives of the Croat Democratic Union deemed that the referendum question should also incorporate the question, saying that Bosnia-Herzegovina would, in the future, be organised along the cantonal alliance, that it would be cantonised, that is, decentralised. However, when this came to that question, that is, whether it should also make part of the referendum, no agreement was reached between the representatives of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Party for Democratic Action, and at last, they agreed to adopt the question of independence for the referendum and try to resolve the matter of the internal organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina as quickly as possible, that is, organised, as I have said, on the cantonal principle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, we know, sir, that the referendum was held on the 29th of February and March the 1st of 1992. Some contention or some suggestion has been made in this case to the effect that Croats boycotted the referendum on the first day, which was a Saturday, and only voted on the second day, after they had supposedly been instructed to do so by the Catholic church. Could you give the Trial Chamber a feel for whether that assessment is accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: I was, in fact, the secretary of the municipal commission for the organisation of the referendum, and I can say that for the first time since I grew of age, it was the first time that it was decided to hold the referendum on a Saturday, because votes, elections, always took place on Sundays. So people found it unusual and somewhat strange. So in principle, people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially at that time, would be at their jobs five days, and Saturday and Sunday were used for shopping or for all sorts of household chores. Therefore, they were planning to attend the referendum, to turn out for the referendum on Sunday. I believe, and I was a participant in this, the turnout on Saturday -- both Croats and Muslims turned up in small numbers on Saturday but then on Sunday it was decisive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were the Busovaca municipality secretary for the commission -- of the commission for the referendum; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your responsibilities in that regard, Mr. Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The task of the municipal commission was to organise the voting at the referendum so that all citizens could come out and vote and then to establish the results of the referendum in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'd just like to show you one exhibit that's already been introduced into evidence, with the usher's assistance. It's D74/1. Mr. Grubesic, this appears to be a petition signed by residents of Busovaca in favour of the referendum on independence. Do you recognise the document?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this document. This was indeed being done. A questionnaire or, rather, a petition was signed, and I am positive that you can find my name on this list. I have no time to look for it at the moment, but I recognise very many names here in this list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you just take a look at the last page of the document, the very last page with the yellow tab on it. Is that the page that you signed?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my signature and the number of my identity card.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that the petition was signed by Croats, Muslims and Serbs, all of whom were resident in the municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except that I think that Serbs didn't turn out in large numbers, but I also believe that there were Serbs who signed this petition and also members of other ethnic groups, that is, apart from Croats, Muslims, and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. It's fair to say, I think, that the vote was overwhelmingly in favour of independence.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the referendum on independence to succeed, two-thirds of Bosnian nationals had to vote for -- had to vote yes, and that was achieved, and the results were similar across Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Busovaca too. As far as I can remember, the highest turnout was in the municipality of Siroki Brijeg, which is a municipality with a Croat majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the country have become independent without the Croat vote, sir? Could it have met the two-thirds majority required?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since the majority of Serbs were against the referendum, not all of them but a considerable number, without Croat votes, the Muslims alone would not have been able to vote for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, simply in light of the ethnic structure in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I'll take the witness quickly through paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe your country announced its independence on March the 6th of 1992, and shortly thereafter, the JNA and Bosnian Serb army launched attacks against the city of Mostar in mid-March and surrounded and besieged the capital, Sarajevo, just a few weeks later. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe it's also accurate to say that the JNA and BSA seized about 70 per cent of the entire territory of your country, resulting in many thousands of people being killed and hundreds of thousands of people being forced out of their homes to become displaced persons or refugees.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, these facts are accurate too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Grubesic. Let me turn away from the general subjects that are addressed in your outline, and I'd like to turn to the specific facts that are pertinent to charges against Mr. Kordic here. How long have you known Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have known Mr. Kordic since 1986 or 1987, from the time when I worked in the Busovaca municipality's land records office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber a little bit about Mr. Kordic's family?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kordic family is a renowned family in Busovaca. His father, Pero Kordic, was a veterinarian for a number of years in Busovaca, and his mother was a paediatrician in the health centre in Busovaca and has worked there for a number of years also. In addition to his mother and father, Mr. Kordic has three sisters and a brother, and I know all family members. So this is a family of a physician and a veterinarian who have been renowned or well known throughout Busovaca because they assisted a lot of people. Unfortunately, Mr. Kordic's mother is gravely ill, and her husband, Mr. Kordic's father, Mr. Pero Kordic, is caring for her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned that you first became acquainted with Mr. Kordic during your work in the land records office of the municipality. Could you tell the Trial Chamber the circumstances under which you first became acquainted with Mr. Kordic and what he was known for, if anything, at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, Mr. Kordic came to the land records office to resolve certain issues. He was trying to build a house with his wife, Venera, who is an educator. The issue was not a very serious one. We resolved it. It had to do with getting a building permit. He was able to get a building permit. This is how we first met. It was a business contact, an official business. Then I learned that Mr. Kordic was an in-house reporter at a local company called Vatrostalna. I learned that he was a journalist, that he studied political science, and that he got the job in the town where he grew up. Later on, in conversations with other people, I learned that Mr. Kordic was fairly active in his company, that he was involved in trying to improve the working conditions, and he was helping everyone, regardless of their ethnic background, to improve their status. I'm a year or two senior to Mr. Kordic, but I was impressed by him as an educated young man. Very bright, very polite, who also came back to his hometown after his education was completed, to come and help out, and we got along quite well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I believe, sir, that both you and he joined the HDZ-BiH in the summer of 1990.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've already described after the election how Mr. Kordic was appointed to the office of -- or appointed to be the municipal secretary of the defence office. What was his job in that regard? Could you please let the Trial Chamber know? And, also, could you give some indication, since it uses the word "defence," was this a civilian position or was it a military position in any sense?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to comment very briefly on what was the competence of these Municipal Secretariat of Defence which is what the name used to be. By law, the law provided that the municipalities had to have these secretariats and they had to finance them also. These offices registered all the potential draftees so they also had personal files of people who had served in the military. So these were the two major roles that the secretariats had. Also, if a JNA unit wanted to raise the levels of their conscripts, then it would be -- this would be done through the secretariat, and their role in this process was purely administrative. It is for the recruitment of conscripts, and also I want to add that these conscripts would go to medical exam, and an official from the secretariat would organise this and take them there. And that would be -- that was the end of his role in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me see if I've understood that. His role was to keep personal files on potential members of the JNA, is this right, and also those who had served?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the role in relation to the conscripts, which I haven't entirely followed, what was his role in relation to conscripts?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't -- I answered very briefly in order not to waste the Court's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't change your mind on that. Just tell us briefly what it is he did.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the law, when a young man reached 17 years of age, they had to go and register with the Secretariat of Defence because the secretariat did not keep records of who was 17. So they would announce through the public media or send out circular letters to everyone in the population and these young men would then respond and come to the office and register. After they reached 18 years, they -- the secretariat was obligated to call them and then, according to prearranged plan, to transport them, to provide them transportation to the medical examination board which would then review their ability or fitness for military service. So for them, the role was to gather these young men and bring them to the place where the medical examination board would meet. That was their role there and the medical commission would take over. Then they would wait until the end of this examination and then they would bring them back and they would also handle the medical records, that is, the personal medical files of these potential recruits, conscripts, and then if -- when the JNA asked for a certain number of new recruits to go and serve in the JNA, then they would handle those requests and they would send out the requested number of young conscripts to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's enough.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was this a civilian position or was it a military position, Mr. Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a civilian position. At that time, the secretary of the Secretariat of Defence was appointed by the municipal government. This would be a civilian employee. They would come to work wearing civilian clothes and they would be on the payroll of the civilian administrative staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Turning to paragraph 29, Mr. Grubesic, we've heard a lot about the strategic importance of Central Bosnia and the fact that it was home to a number of arms ammunitions manufacturing factories, for example, in Vitez, Novi Travnik, Konjic, Bugojno and elsewhere. Do you, yourself, have you any knowledge of, have you had any connections with any of these arms ammunitions manufacturing facilities during your professional political career?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether I had any contacts with any of these manufacturers, is that the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Have you had any role in connection with the arms ammunitions factories in the towns I've just cited or during the course of your career?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Has the witness got his statement in front of him?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I can't --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the statement that you have in front of you, Mr. Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, from now on, you better put that away, please, and give your evidence without the assistance of that. If at some stage you need to look at your statement to remember a date or something of that sort, then of course you can refer to it. But I think from now on, we better have your evidence without that assistance. Mr. Sayers, as far as these arms factories are concerned, we've had a great deal of evidence about it and I don't think we need to go on to that but certainly go -- you could -- the background, I think, is probably fully known to us, unless there's something you want to explore particularly. It seems paragraph 31 is where we should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, I fully agree, Mr. President, and that's where we'll go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Grubesic, could you tell us whether Mr. Kordic was elected to or appointed to any other political position in the Busovaca branch of the Croat Democratic Union in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, Mr. Dario Kordic was appointed the secretary of the HDZ-BiH branch in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he ever appointed president at any time of the Busovaca HDZ-BiH as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1991, he was appointed the president of the Busovaca branch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell the Court whether the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina ever took a position with respect to conscription of young men residing in the country into the JNA?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991, and I don't know whether this was in mid-1991 or in the latter part of 1991 but, in any event, they adopted a decision not to send new conscripts from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And his role at secretary of the defence office in Busovaca, did Mr. Kordic play any role, as far as you're aware, in connection with that decision on the part of the Presidency of the country?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kordic implemented this decision of the Presidency together with other officials who worked in the defence office. They did not send conscripts to the JNA conforming to the decision of the Presidency, and this was the case in all municipalities where Croats were in the majority or where Croats and Muslims formed the majority. There was a danger that the JNA would forcibly take control of these personnel files and in many places, including Busovaca, these files were then moved out of these offices. A special problem was the young conscripts who were from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and other parts of the former Yugoslavia who were already serving in the JNA. The JNA did not recognise this decision of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and did not allow soldiers from those territories to go back home. Many escaped and would go to -- would show up in different towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina seeking assistance, and officials in the local governments helped a number of such young soldiers to acquire civilian clothes and be able to return to their homes. There were such cases in Busovaca too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Was there any effort made to obstruct the export of locally manufactured weapons at the Bratstvo factory, for example, or explosives from the Slobodan Princip factory in Vitez to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was clear that the weapons manufactured in the various plants in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Central Bosnia, there were several of them which employed people of all three ethnic groups and there were efforts to stop the export of such weapons or delivery of such weapons to the JNA where it would be used in the war in Croatia, and several of such convoys were blocked and stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you let the Trial Chamber know, and this is moving forward to paragraph 32, Your Honours, whether Mr. Kordic played any individual role or any visible role in these efforts to halt or obstruct the process of JNA armed convoys.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, Dario Kordic, together with other people from Central Bosnia who saw clearly what these weapons were used for, took part in these attempts to prevent weapons from leaving Central Bosnia and to be used by the JNA against Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You've referred to an arms convoy in September of 1991, taking arms from Travnik towards Sarajevo. Could you give the Trial Court your recollection of the role that Mr. Kordic played in connection with that convoy, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the latter part of September 1991, a convoy filled with weapons and ammunition was moving from Travnik towards Sarajevo and was stopped at Kaonik. Citizens of several municipalities in Central Bosnia took part in this, including Mr. Dario Kordic. He courageously stepped in front of these vehicles and told them to stop and not take these weapons there which would kill people, and he wanted the war in Croatia stop to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did incidents like that have any impact upon Mr. Kordic's perception or standing in the local community, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such courageous acts of Mr. Dario Kordic with bare arms, he stepped and resisted the fourth largest military force, as it was alleged, in Europe at the time. This increased his reputation among the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to skip over paragraph 33 and 34, Your Honour, because I think we've already heard about that generally and specifically from this witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to April the 2nd of 1992. I'm going to paragraph 35 now. Mr. Grubesic, on April the 2nd of 1992, I think you were appointed to be secretary of the ten-member Busovaca Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what that entity was, what the Crisis Staff was, and what its function was? Why was it appointed?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was popularly known, the Crisis Staff, but the official name is -- the name was the Presidency of the Municipal Assembly in the State of War or Imminent Threat of War. It was appointed by the Municipal Assembly of Busovaca, according to the law, and it was a multi-party body. Members of all parties which had council people in the assembly made up this Crisis Staff. It included Croats, Muslims, and Serbs. Its task was to prepare the municipality, as best it could, for a potential but clearly pending threat of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the Crisis Staff have any duties or tasks in connection with the three JNA barracks that were located in the Busovaca area, the Draga barracks, the Kaonik barracks, and the Kacuni barracks?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The task of the Crisis Staff was to organise all activities in the territory of the municipality in accordance with the threat of war, and also to reach agreements with the JNA for the JNA to move out of the three barracks in Busovaca municipality which you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the Court has heard some evidence of this, Mr. Grubesic, but was there an arrangement reached between the Croat communities and the Muslim communities in your municipality regarding what was to happen to the arms located in these three barracks, and if so, in your own words could you tell the Trial Chamber exactly what those arrangements were?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this agreement was formalised, that is, set down in writing, but this agreement was reached. It did not involve only the weapons but also the takeover of the facilities, because it was assumed that the majority of weapons had been pulled out of these barracks, especially Draga and Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was to take control of the Draga barracks?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was that the Croats would take control of the Draga barracks; and the Muslims of the Kacuni barracks; and as far as the Kaonik barracks is concerned, it was to be taken over by the Croats but that the weapons would be divided in equal parts approximately between the Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, was there an incident on April the 26th of 1992 following the withdrawal of the JNA from the Draga barracks?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On 26 April 1992, after the departure on part of the JNA soldiers from the Draga barracks, there was heavy shelling of Busovaca, actually, heavy bombing of Busovaca by the JNA air force. This was sheer -- these were sheer reprisals, and a number of civilians were killed in the town. A number of facilities and structures were damaged, including the hospital, which was clearly marked with a Red Cross sign, and it was heavily damaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me just move forward in time to May the 9th of 1992. Could you tell the Court where you were on that day, as far as you can recall, and what happened?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On 9 May, 1992, I was on duty in the Crisis Staff of Busovaca in the afternoon, and because of the continued threats of air attacks, the Crisis Staff moved its offices to the basement of the PTT building. So that's where I was on the afternoon of May 9.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you receive any telephone calls from anyone during that duty shift?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During my shift in the afternoon - actually, it was already dusk -- a call came from the Kaonik barracks that the JNA wanted to withdraw its troops and their personal weapons, and they were ready to leave for Zenica or some other previously agreed-to location, and the president of the Crisis Staff was supposed to come and take over the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, I called Mr. Zoran Maric, and I cannot recall whether I called him from home or whether there was Vinko Miljag, but in any event, we went to -- on behalf of the Crisis Staff, we went to the Draga barracks to do this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber what happened while you were at the Draga barracks talking to the JNA officers that had called you.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were talking about the JNA officer in the Draga barracks, we saw that the soldiers there were fully armed and getting ready to go, and they were starting to show us the building where the soldiers were staying. Then this officer received a call to go and attend a meeting outside of the barracks. When he left the barracks, the shooting started around the barracks. The soldiers in the barracks quickly assumed positions in the trenches where they were prepared there and asked us what was going on. We couldn't tell them. We didn't know what was going on. At that time, our lives were in danger, the three civilians that were there. We thought that perhaps the word had gotten out that these soldiers were leaving so that the celebration had started outside or something. We didn't know. Afterwards, this noncommissioned JNA officer came to the barracks, and the decision was taken that they would not leave that night but, rather, another time. The shooting, meanwhile, had subsided and we left the barracks. It was already dark. I don't know what time it was, but it could have been about 2100 hours, perhaps even later. I went on to -- I continued home, because at this time my shift was over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And was anyone wounded during this outbreak of shooting that you heard that evening?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later I learned that a Croatian man called Darko Vuleta was seriously wounded and that a Muslim was seriously wounded. I don't know this person's name now. They both were seriously wounded. I also later heard that there was an incident between the HVO and the TO at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have submitted an affidavit from Ivo Brnada which corroborates that particular contention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving on, sir, you said that you went home on the evening of May the 9th, 1992. What did you do the next day?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day, unaware what had happened that night, I once again set off to work at the Crisis Staff in the basement of the PTT office in Busovaca; however, when I arrived, I saw that there was no one there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had anyone come to work since the aerial bombardment of Busovaca on April the 26th that you've previously described?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the crisis staff had moved to the post office fearing the danger of JNA air attack, nobody worked in the building or the municipal hall in Busovaca nor did parties come there. Otherwise, there was already a mayhem, very many people, children, women had fled to Republic of Croatia. It was a very difficult, a very confused situation. All the municipal services did not really work nor did anybody turn to them for help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just turn to the next subject, Mr. Grubesic, which concerns the establishment of the HVO administration in Busovaca and the operation of the HVO government up until basically the outbreak of fighting in Busovaca in January of 1993. Could you tell the Trial Chamber whether life gradually returned to normal after May 10th of 1992 in the municipality or whether it did not.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th of May, 1992, the JNA left the Kaonik barracks in daytime. It was the 10th of May. I think it was the 10th of May, and there were no JNA soldiers in the territory of Busovaca municipality anymore. There was this constant danger of air attacks by the JNA air force, but people had already run out of food, and some necessities began to be more acute so this life had to be organised. One had to gradually enable people to begin to shop, to have the shops open, to have the services back in operation again. That is, in that first wave, people had bought up all the stocks that the shops held so there were no more stocks there, and life had to be organised normally once again. That was when we began to think once again about the reinstatement of the municipal government, rather beginning of work of municipal civil servants. Needless to say, those who had already been called up either for the army of Bosnia -- that is Territorial Defence or the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in connection with the reestablishment of life in the municipality, did the municipality undertake any duties or responsibilities in connection with the logistical supply of your troops on the front lines with the Bosnian Serb army or the JNA?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever the case, the municipality provided the troops with logistics, as much as it could, with fuel and food and everything else, because it was evident that there was no system or rather the state which would back up the soldiers defending the area so that the municipalities had to bear the brunt of it or rather municipalities became small states.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, actually one of the municipal governments in these unsettled circumstances that you've just described where the central government had essentially stopped functioning, couldn't support the operations of its municipalities, was there any distinction or differentiation between the civilian and the military authorities within the -- or at the municipality level in the very earliest days that we're talking about, spring of 1992, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you. At that time, everything was in disarray. What we had organised was the municipal government. All the rest had to be built and, at that time, when you do not have any clear regulations, any clear instructions, then there was a lot of overlapping. Some people knew how to organise authority, some didn't, and the conditions were practically impossible. They precluded any kind of normal work. I should give you an example. In the municipality, we believed that we had to wear uniforms because the war affects everybody including us, but then the ECMM warned us that the civilian authorities should wear civilian clothes so the -- so for the first 10 or 15 days, we wore uniforms to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the question was: Was there ever a differentiation between civilian and military authorities within the municipality? Could you give us your understanding of the answer to that question, sir, since you were there?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were trying to enjoy a difference between them and we did; however, it wasn't always possible to distinguish the two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Moving on to paragraph 40, and we have some documents that we have to go through, six documents, Your Honour, in connection with this paragraph. Let me just address the substance of it first. There's a contention made in this case that, sir, the reorganised administration in Busovaca after 1992 discriminated against Bosnian Muslims. Could you give the Trial Chamber your views on whether those allegations have any substance or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that such claims have no substance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall say the following: When the municipality went back to work, all of the municipal civil servants were invited to come back to their jobs regardless of their ethnicity. And all municipal civil servants came back to work. Some, some said they had already been mobilised either by the HVO or the BH army, but they were still on the municipal payroll and they were getting their salary there, but they did not come to their work places in the municipal hall because they were discharging the duties in the army. Some women with children of up to seven were entitled to a leave in wartime, and those women were also on the municipal payroll, stayed at home and looked after their children. And everybody else came to work in the municipal hall in Busovaca, and I believe that documentation in the municipality of Busovaca could -- there is a decision which says that everybody should go back to the jobs they held before the outbreak of war, those who had stayed there. And most people had stayed there. Very few people had left the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina to Serbia or Montenegro. So everybody went back to their old jobs, the exception being three or four persons who were substituted, who replaced those people who had left to Serbia or Montenegro. But practically everybody went back to their old jobs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any requirement for these people who were returning to work to swear oaths of loyalty or sign oaths of loyalty to the HZ HB or the HVO, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for the Trial Chamber's reference, I believe the witness was referring to the Exhibit Z111A from May 22, 1992, an order instructing people to return to work. Have you ever seen a kind of written loyalty of this type, Mr. Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think -- no, I don't think that happened in the municipality of Busovaca. Besides, I don't think it was necessary, and that will be a discriminatory act. I don't think it could occur to anyone to request such statements from anybody. Those people used to work there before, and they had all the right to continue working in those jobs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any form established for discussion of things such as the production of goods necessary to survive the winter; health services, mobilisation of the community's assets, school issues, things of that variety or were the two communities, three communities, Bosnian Croat, Bosnian Serb and Bosnian Muslim simply not speaking about those matters with one another?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to say what I told you until now. We cannot speak about some ideal or idyllic situation at the time. It was wartime and the situation was very difficult. But, we were trying to find some way, some means to ensure that people of all the ethnic origins could stay and live in that area. And my information is as early as June, a meeting took place among the representatives of the leaders of the chief parties or if you like, prominent citizens of all ethnic groups, who reached an understanding about all these matters that you have just raised, and meetings of the representatives of the two communities, if I may put it rather crudely, but two ethnic communities met regularly and they discussed the most important issues. When it came to operative matters, then it was put through by the municipal government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Grubesic, I'd like to go over a set of documents with you. These are by no means exhaustive, there's been a huge amount of documents in this case, but they will serve as good examples over a fairly broad span of time of the negotiations or discussions that were occurring between the communities. The first document is dated June 27, 1992 and it may be, indeed, a document that reflects what you've just testified about. With the Trial Chamber's permission, I'd like to have this marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document will be marked D223/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if we could have a copy of the English version put on the ELMO, page one, first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Grubesic, these appear to be a record or this document appears to be a record of a meeting that occurred between the two communities on June the 25th, 1992, and the introduction says: "Guided by the fact that the Croatian people has always held that each people has a right to freedom and free expression of its own interests and that there is a possibility of coexistence in mixed communities, this being a historical fact in these parts ..." and so on. We can all read what it says. Is this the meeting that you had in mind when you just testified about the bilateral discussions occurring between the Croat and Muslim communities in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is only one in a series of meetings of this nature, when representatives of ethnic communities in the territory of the municipality of Busovaca met. I know this document. I have also seen it before. So I think that it says what I have already told you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. It was attended by Mr. Kordic and Mr. Glavocevic and Mr. Stipac on the Croat side, and by the identified people from the Muslim National Council on the Muslim side. Paragraph 1 states that: "The Croatian people respect the sovereignty of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina but at the same time respect the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." Did you ever hear, during the entire duration of the civil war after this time, sir, anyone ever expressing views that undermined a recognition of the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard such statements, and that was a period of time when a large number of the states involved had recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent and sovereign state. So I do not think that it would have been politically wise to do anything like that or, at any rate, I know that no Croats and no Muslims ever did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And the second paragraph states that the supreme command in Busovaca would be the HVO, but that did not preclude the autonomy of formations of the Territorial Defence or TO within the HVO. Did you ever hear anybody express views that were contrary to that particular idea after June the 27th of 1992, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In point of fact, this item was never operationalised. The Croat Defence Council and the units of the Territorial Defence, that is, BH army, continued to operate autonomously of each other. So there was no subordination or, rather, attachment, which I believe is the military term.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The third paragraph goes on to say that the joint operation of the military police of the TO and of the HVO is not possible because the pre-conditions for it are not in place, but that the situation with respect to the military police is a temporary one due to the large number of soldiers engaged in the TO and the HVO. It is correct, is it not, that at this time there were large numbers of soldiers in the TO and the HVO in June of 1992, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the paragraph goes on to say that the TO military police would continue to police the entirely Muslim villages, while the HVO military police would police the other areas. Is that your understanding of the situation that prevailed after June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By and large, that was the situation as of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could just ask the usher to put the second page on the ELMO. There are just a few points of interest here. As you've previously testified, sir, the perception was that the Croat people had mobilised earlier than the Muslims, taken the threat of military aggression on the part of the JNA and BSA more seriously, and that's reflected in paragraph 5, I believe.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But certainly the HVO recognised the right of the Muslim people to mobilise and have its representatives join the TO and to send them to any of the battlefields in the republic. Is that the case or is it not?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. I already said that there was a major danger, very many people were killed, the last part of the territory was conquered by the army of Bosnian Serbs, and every soldier, therefore, had to commit himself in order to prevent any such further crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next item of interest is paragraph 7, sir, which says that the municipal HVO of Busovaca was always open to a certain number of representatives of the Muslim people. Were there any Muslim representatives on the HVO government of the municipality of Busovaca at this time?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Without documents I cannot really tell you exactly, but even before this agreement, or perhaps in the wake of it, that is what was done, and I think that in practice, this -- that this was already the practice even before this agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then this agreement is signed by Mr. Glavocevic as the president of the HVO in the municipality of Busovaca. How long did he remain president of the HVO in Busovaca, if you can remember, Mr. Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was there until the 27th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who replaced him at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was replaced by Mr. Zoran Maric. He was the president -- he was mayor of the municipality of Busovaca, elected in lawful elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Maric retain that position as president of the Busovaca municipal HVO for the duration of the civil war?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The next short document I'd like to show you, sir, is dated July the 15th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'd like to have this marked as an exhibit too, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D224/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Mr. Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that your signature on the document, the Croatian original?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. This gives you authority to issue passes and clearances for traffic and goods to persons residing in the municipality of Busovaca; is that right? Along with Mr. Glavocevic, that is.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I could, as a matter of fact, sign only in the absence of Mr. Glavocevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this a military function at all, the ability to sign passes, or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Movement of persons and traffic in goods is an exclusively civilian matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The third of the six documents I'd like you to review is dated July the 22nd of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document will be marked D225/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Grubesic, please don't think that these are all the documents. These are just a representative sample over a period of time. This document, sir, apparently is dated July the 22nd, 1992, and reflects discussions between a number of people concerning the reconstruction of a road from Pavlovic to Gornji Vakuf and the necessity of rounding up people and machinery to do Busovaca's part of handling this job. One of the people present was Senad Ekmescic. Was he a Muslim or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Senad Ekmescic is a Muslim by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see that along the line of people to be sent a copy of this is Mr. Ekmescic but also, in item number 7, Mr. Husein Hadzimejlic, he being the person you previously identify as the TO commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President this, might be an appropriate time for the break just before we get into the other three documents, or I can take the three other documents in short order if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now. Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, you've got another three witnesses you want this week; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It is. I regret to say, Your Honour, I think we are going to run into some scheduling problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's move as quickly as we can through this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I will try to do that, Your Honour. The next document, Mr. Grubesic, I'd like you to look at is dated August 3, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D226/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Grubesic, this document relates to a meeting with the directors of commercial enterprises on August 3, 1992 attended by you and, amongst others, Mr. Ekmescic. Just a couple of points. With respect to item four, enterprises would have to submit to both the HVO and TO military units lists of requisitioned motor vehicles and request return of the vehicles which were not indispensable to the military. Do you recall the subject of this discussion with representatives of commercial enterprises throughout the municipality?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was a very important meeting with the senior economic executives for discussing of these issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I notice that Mr. Zoran Maric is the acting president of the HVO in Busovaca municipality as of this time. Is that your recollection too?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one final point, on the second page of the document, item number 11 and 12, problems regarding traffic, currency and banks have been emphasised and it was also decided that it was important that uniform crisis be imposed for basic staples throughout the municipality. Do you recall any discussion of those issues?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was discussed and the agreements were reached and the appropriate conclusions set out as reflected in these two items.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And once again representatives of both communities participating in the discussions and having their input taken into account as resolutions for --

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be more accurate to say that the representatives of all three communities discussed these issues because one of the presidents was Milutan Stanicic [phoen], who was an ethnic Serb, who was one of the managers, not the chief executive officer, but one of the top executives in the largest company in town Medijapan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The next document I would like you to review is about a month later, September 4, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be D227/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a few questions about this document, sir. You were listed as one of the attendees. Do you recall this meeting on September 4th, 1992, a meeting of the executive committee HDZ-BiH held in Busovaca on that day?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall this meeting and I did attend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A number of political and military issues were discussed. One thing I would like to draw to your attention is on the first page where it says "AD-2", the observation was made that people had been poorly informed about issues vital for Busovaca municipality and because of the executive committee of the HDZ felt it important to organise meetings with individuals in villages to explain the current situation. A number of those people in the field were identified as, amongst others, Mr. Kordic and you. But also, it was observed or decided that the military commander should be present at these meetings too. Now, by this time, sir, September 4th of 1992, had the military institutions largely separated from the civilian institutions and developed their own chain of command as far as you're aware or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot assess how much they had developed the chain of command but the situation was getting more and more organised, and the competencies of the military and civilian authorities were being separated and distinguished. But this was still not enough, so we couldn't say that all the full organisation was reached. There was progress, but not enough was done, not by a long shot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And down at the bottom of the first page of the Croatian and first at the top of the second page of the English, the observation went on that the explanation and information should be provided by Dario, Mr. Kordic, I take it; Ignac, Mr. Kostroman; Tiho, Colonel Blaskic; Sekerija, presumably Luka Sekerija; Floro, Mr. Glavocevic; Stipac, Mr. Anto Stipac; Zoran Maric, and you. And then the plan of visits and explanations would be made by the military commanders. Could you just tell the Court who were the military commanders?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Busovaca, the military commander of the brigade was Mr. Dusko Grubesic, I believe that it was around that time that he became the president. I don't know the exact date, but I know that for the most part in 1992 and 1993, Mr. Dusko Grubesic was the commander of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right at the end of the document, sir, there's reference to a commission for urgent negotiations, which was to invite, urgently, Muslim representatives to talks and to try to reach agreements on all disputed issues in the area of the municipality of Busovaca, and on that commission would be Mr. Kordic, Mr. Maric, Mr. Stipac, and Mr. Glavocevic. Do you recall decisions being made along those lines?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was agreed in this meeting that such meetings should be organised in order to resolve some outstanding issues. One was the beginning of the school year, because this was April of 1993. This was the usual time for the resumption of the school activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In connection with the resumption of the school year, the next document I would like you to look at is one, I believe, that you signed, sir, dated September the 10th, 1992, which I'd like to have marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document will be marked D228/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Grubesic, is that your signature on this document as the note-taker?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this document represents negotiations between representatives of the three ethnic communities that comprise the population of Busovaca, and refers to decisions that were made regarding the school curriculum and the language to be used; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is about the negotiations between the Croats and the Muslims, and the rest that you said is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, for example, makes certain decisions relating to the literature to be taught at the schools, and a resolution that for the most part, the books that would be used as part of the syllabus would have to encompass authors from both nationalities, Croat and Muslim.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in addition, it was emphasised that the culture, language, and literature of one or the other of the two nationalities is common and, therefore, each nation would have a right to call its mother tongue by its own name.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That takes us to September, Mr. Grubesic. Let me move forward in time to October of 1992, and one more document dated October the 6th, 1992, concerning negotiations between representatives of the various parties. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I could have this marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D229/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Grubesic, this relates to a meeting attended by representatives, it appears, of the Muslim community and the Croat community, on the 6th of October, 1992, and a significant debate that occurred concerning departure of the Serb population from the territory of the municipality of Busovaca and other issues relating to the passage of Serb refugees through the territory of Busovaca. Do you recall this meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was a note-taker of this meeting, and my signature is at the bottom of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you'd turn to page 3. We can all read what else is in the document. Would it be fair to say that this was a pretty vigorous debate between the two communities, sir, Croat and Muslim?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the Serbs. This meeting was held between -- with the representatives of three communities taking part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see that one of the participants on page 3 here is Mr. Huseinspahic, a Muslim. He was actually a member of the government of the Busovaca municipality, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his responsibility, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the head of one of the agencies in the municipal government. I cannot recall which one, but he was head of one of the agencies there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he -- were his duties real duties or, to use a phrase, was he a token representative of the Muslim community on the HVO government in that sense? Could you tell the Court which of those two versions is accurate?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His duties were real, like everybody else's who was employed there. Everybody had to perform at work. We were very few, and we all had to work. So Mr. Huseinspahic had real duties as he had real rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. There's a reference on page 3, under Mr. Maric, who makes certain proposals regarding the passage of Serb people from Zenica and Kakanj and so forth being permitted to pass through Busovaca municipality, a proposal which, incidentally, was approved by both Croats and Muslims. Is that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Maric proposed this, and these were actually the conclusions adopted by this meeting which was held on 6th October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some witnesses in this case, sir, have contended or claimed that per capita transit charges were imposed upon these unfortunate people of Serb ethnicity to travel through Busovaca municipality from Zenica. Is there any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No official contributions were paid or fees were paid. I cannot say whether individuals asked for some fees for their private transportation arrangements. That I don't know. But that was not official.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. In terms of charging every single Serb person passing through the municipality as a point of HDZ or HVO policy, is there any truth that that occurred, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. I said that some, not all Serbs, but I heard that some people were asked to pay for this service, for the transportation which they were provided with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was this by members --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think you've got the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. I think you're right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last document in this series, sir, is dated November the 10th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D230/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not many questions about this, sir. Once again, a joint body convened, Muslims and Croats on it, among them Mr. Huseinspahic, the Muslim representative of the government; and Mr. Husnija Neslanovic, the Muslim chief of police; and Mr. Hadzimejlic, the TO commander. Do you recall this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall this meeting. It was held on 10 November 1992, and I was a note-taker at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the agenda, as item 1, is activities related to the establishment of a joint command of the HVO and the ABiH. Was that issue discussed?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any resolutions taken or action taken towards achievement of that item that was under discussion?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusion reached in this meeting was to establish a joint command when such a decision comes from the higher authorities, either civilian or military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As of this time, sir, November the 10th, 1992, is it your understanding that the TO or ABiH and HVO were both legal armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Did you say on the 2nd -- on the 10th of February or the 10th of November?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As of the 10th of November, 1992. Sorry if I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to the information I have, further to the regulations of Bosnia and Herzegovina, both ABiH, the HVO, and the police of Bosnia and Herzegovina formed the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Three brief points relating to this document. Paragraph 3, sir, says that new refugees and displaced persons would be received as permitted by housing capacities available in houses and vacation homes and that a member of the commission had to be present at the site. Do you recall that subject being discussed?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was discussed, and this is the conclusion that was adopted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And people, in item 5, refugees and displaced persons would not be subjected to forced evictions from already inhabited houses and vacation homes. Could you tell the Court a little bit about that, sir. What were the circumstances of that resolution?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a large influx of refugees, and there were cases when refugees, that is, displaced persons forcibly moved into abandoned homes or vacation houses, and it was decided then that they would not be forcibly removed, these refugees or displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, conclusions at this meeting, conclusion one and three, first that representatives authorized representatives of both the Croat and Muslim peoples would disavow excesses committed in Busovaca over the public radio both Croat and Muslim radio; Radio Busovaca for the Croats and Radio Zenica for the Muslims. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was agreed because there were a number of excesses, and we wanted to go to the public. And I believe that we publicly went -- we went public on the radio in Busovaca condemning this as representatives of the authority, and which also asked public to support us in our condemnation of such excesses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, "Persons of such duty would not be permitted to wear uniforms or bear arms in the town." Was that your recollection of one of the decisions that was made in the town, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this meeting, we agreed and we continued to try to implement this conclusion that soldiers were -- would only wear uniforms and carry weapons while on duty, because most of them actually slept at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
